title: Why the farthest throw is not the steepest throw

target.failure: The steeper the launch, the farther the ball goes.
target.operation: Split the launch velocity into a part that carries the ball along and a part that keeps it in the air, and see that the range needs both.
target.invariant: Launch angles that add up to 90 degrees land the ball at the same distance, and no angle beats 45 degrees.
target.boundary: The 45 degree rule belongs to level ground with no air resistance; the tempting rule is right at one angle only, by coincidence.

context.situation: A ball is launched from level ground at a fixed speed of 20 m/s. You can change only the angle it leaves at. It flies, and comes down on the ground again.

quantities.label: most range any angle can give

scene.title: The flight, from the side
scene.job: Shows where the ball goes and, one cause at a time, why: the launch velocity split into the part that carries it along and the part that keeps it up.
scene.description: A side view of level ground. A ball leaves the origin at the angle you set, follows a curved path up to a peak and comes down on the ground at a landing point whose distance from the start is the range.

second_view.title: How far it lands, at every angle
second_view.job: Shows the whole pattern at once: the range as the angle changes, which the picture of one flight cannot.
second_view.description: A graph of the range in metres against the launch angle in degrees. The curve rises from a short range at a low angle to a peak and falls again at steep angles. A dashed line marks the most any angle can give.

predict.prompt: The ball always leaves at 20 m/s and you choose only the angle. As you raise the angle from 5° to 85°, what will happen to how far it lands?

options.text: It lands farther every time the launch is steeper, right up to 85°.

tests.says: At {theta:0}° it lands only {R:1} m away, closer than a 45° launch.

options.text: It lands farther at first, there is a longest distance somewhere in between, and then it lands closer again.
It lands the same distance whatever the angle, because the speed is the same.

tests.says: At {theta:0}° it lands {R:1} m away; a 30° launch lands much farther.

goals.prompt: Find a launch angle that lands the ball more than 38 m away.
goals.hint: Try angles in the middle of the range.

goals.prompt: Now find a LOW launch, under 20°, that still lands more than 12 m away.
goals.hint: Low launches go further than you might think.

goals.prompt: Find a very steep launch, over 75°, and read where it lands.
goals.hint: Steep launches spend their time going up and down.

statements.text: Every time the launch gets steeper, the ball lands farther.
statements.why: It is true below 45° and false above it: the range rises to a peak and then falls.

statements.text: The longest range comes from a launch at 45°.
statements.why: The range depends on sin 2θ, which is largest when 2θ is 90°.

statements.text: Launches at 30° and 60° land at the same distance.
statements.why: Angles that add up to 90° give sin 2θ the same value.

statements.text: A launch at 80° goes higher than one at 45° and also lands farther.
statements.claim: at(H, theta, 80) > at(H, theta, 45) and at(R, theta, 80) > at(R, theta, 45)
statements.why: A steeper launch goes higher but spends its time going up and down, not along.

contradict.imposes: Suppose the ball landed farther the steeper you launched, as if the range simply grew with the sine of the angle.

goal.prompt: Find a launch angle where this tempting model is wrong by more than 20 m.

contradict.why_correct: Tilting the launch up shrinks the horizontal speed while it lengthens the time in the air; the product rises and then falls.
contradict.why_wrong: The tempting model counts only the time in the air and forgets that a steeper launch has less horizontal speed to cover the ground with.

steps.text: The launch velocity: one arrow along the direction you chose.
Split it. The horizontal part carries the ball along the ground at a steady rate.
The vertical part is slowed by gravity, stops at the peak and reverses.

ask.prompt: Which part of the velocity decides how long the ball stays in the air?
ask.why: Gravity acts only on the vertical motion: the time up and down is 2·vy/g whatever the horizontal speed.

steps.text: So the vertical part sets the time in the air, and the horizontal part decides how far the ball gets in that time.
The horizontal speed stays the same all through the flight.
The vertical speed at the start.
Time in the air: up and down again at rate g.
Range = horizontal speed × time in the air.

equation.text: Put them together: the range depends on sin 2θ.

invariants.text: Launch angles that add up to 90° land at the same distance.
invariants.try: Pick an angle, then the angle that is 90° minus it, and compare the two ranges.

invariants.text: No angle lands the ball farther than v²/g.
invariants.try: Move through every angle and watch for a range above the dashed line on the graph.

oracles.text: The landing point drawn is at the range R.
The two component arrows drawn add up to half the launch speed.
The launch arrow ends where its horizontal component ends.

boundary.assumption: The ground is level and the air does no work on the ball.
boundary.learner_must_identify: The tempting rule is right at one angle only, 60°, by coincidence; it cannot be used as a rule.

cases.text: Launch at 60°. Does the tempting rule give the true range?

fade.prompt: The ball is launched at 40°. How far does it land? The numbers on the picture are hidden now.
A ball is launched at 25°. At what other angle would it land the same distance? The mechanism and the equation are hidden now.
fade.why: Angles that add up to 90° land at the same distance: {answer:0}° and {theta:0}°.

fade.prompt: One ball is launched at 70°, another at 45°. How much farther does the 45° ball land? Only the physical scene is left.
fade.why: The 45° launch gives the longest range; at {theta:0}° much of the speed is spent going up instead of along. The difference is {answer:1} m.

transfer.prompt: A ball is launched at 15 m/s, 20° above level ground (g = 10 m/s²). How far does it land?
transfer.why: Horizontal speed times the time in the air.
worked: Horizontal speed {vx:2} m/s and vertical speed {vy:2} m/s.

transfer.prompt: A ball launched at 25 m/s at 20° lands at some distance. At what other angle would it land at exactly the same distance?
transfer.why: Launch angles that add up to 90° give the same range.
worked: The two angles add up to 90°.

transfer.prompt: What speed must a ball have, launched at 45°, to land 60 m away? (g = 10 m/s²)
transfer.why: Turn the range rule round: v² = range × g / sin 2θ.
worked: Range = v²·sin 2θ / g, so v² = 60 × {g:0} / sin 2θ.
At {theta:0}° sin 2θ = 1, so v² = 600 and v = {answer:1} m/s.
